analysis.one_liner: Makes union organizing and strikes harder by requiring secret-ballot votes, recertification elections, and dues opt-in.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 154 cosponsors, all Republicans, but was never brought to a vote: it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, received one subcommittee hearing, and died there when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so that unions must win the votes of a majority of all employees in a workplace, not just those who show up to vote, and must be re-elected whenever more than half the workforce turns over. It would require a secret-ballot vote of all affected employees before any strike, and stop unions from spending dues on anything beyond collective bargaining unless each member opts in, in writing, every year. It also adds some protections for individual workers: unions could be penalized for interfering with workers who want to drop representation, and it would criminalize force or threats used to obtain representation rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing campaigns would benefit most: unions that must win every non-voter's implicit support and repeatedly re-win certification would organize less often and bargain with less leverage, which lowers labor costs. Workers who do not want union representation or who object to their dues funding political activity would gain an easier exit and an annual opt-in right.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines a winning union election as a majority of all employees in the bargaining unit, not just a majority of votes cast, so abstentions count against the union.
Requires the NLRB to hold a recertification election whenever more than 50% of a bargaining unit's workforce turns over, with decertification ending the union's contract.

Prohibits any strike unless a majority of all represented employees approve it by secret ballot in an election run by a private organization chosen jointly by the employer and the union, and requires a vote on the employer's offer first.

Bars the use of union dues, fees, or assessments for any purpose beyond collective bargaining unless the employee authorizes it in writing, with authorizations expiring after one year and no automatic renewal.
Gives every employee in a unit, union member or not, the right to vote by secret ballot on ratifying contracts or striking.

Adds penalties on unions that interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees, including over decertification petitions, and makes it a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison to use force or threats to obtain representation rights.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would bear the cost: recertification elections, all-employee vote thresholds, and annual dues re-authorization would shrink membership, revenue, and strike leverage. Unionized workers whose wages, benefits, and job protections rest on collective bargaining would absorb the indirect cost of weaker representation.

drawbacks.text: Counting abstentions as votes against the union means a union could lose an election with, for example, 60% of voters supporting it if turnout is low.

Requiring re-election after 50% workforce turnover would force unions into repeated survival votes in high-turnover industries, which independent analyses of earlier versions of this bill projected would significantly shrink union membership and union revenue.

No strike could begin without a secret-ballot majority of all affected employees in an election whose costs the union bears and whose overseeing organization is chosen jointly with the employer, giving employers a structural role in whether their own workforce strikes.
Requiring annual written re-authorization for dues spent on anything beyond contract administration would cut off the member-funded political and charitable activity unions currently do by default.
Requiring a full NLRB hearing and resolution of every pre-election issue before any union vote could be final would lengthen the organizing process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains genuine individual-worker protections: an annual right to opt in to non-bargaining dues spending, secret-ballot votes on strikes and contracts for all unit employees, penalties on unions that coerce workers, and a new criminal penalty for violent organizing tactics. But its core election rules cut the other way: by counting non-voters against unions, forcing repeated recertification votes in high-turnover workplaces, and requiring an all-employee vote before any strike, the bill would make unions substantially harder to form and keep. The predictable result is less collective bargaining, and the costs of that would fall on workers whose pay and benefits depend on it, while the gains flow to employers in lower labor costs. The framing as an 'employee rights' bill describes the first set of provisions; the second set is the larger structural change.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and was never voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Roe of Tennessee introduced the Employee Rights Act on May 25, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The bill attracted 154 cosponsors, all of them Republicans.
On June 14, 2017, a subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions held a hearing on the bill; that was its only action of substance.
The committee never reported the bill, and the full House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions are better off, since the recertification requirements, all-employee vote thresholds, and dues restrictions never took effect. Employers who would have gained from weaker unions did not get the change.

for.name: Rep. David P. Roe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Employee Rights Act and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: Coalition for Employee Rights
for.role: Business-backed coalition (anchored by the National Federation of Independent Business) supporting the Employee Rights Act
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for the bill's provisions, including workplace recertification elections and union dues opt-in.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral; the committee held one subcommittee hearing but never scheduled a markup or reported the bill to the floor.

against.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Employee Rights Act as an attack on collective bargaining and union membership.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 154 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never reached a floor vote where its support could have been tested.

industries.note: The bill stacks the deck against union survival: abstentions count against unions in elections, unions must be re-elected after 50% workforce turnover, strikes need an all-employee secret-ballot majority, and dues for anything beyond bargaining require annual written opt-in. Union membership, dues revenue, and strike leverage would all shrink, weakening the main channel through which workers bargain over pay and conditions.

industries.industry: Employers in industries with frequent union organizing (retail, hospitality, logistics, manufacturing)
industries.note: Fewer union drives and weaker strike leverage mean lower labor costs and less bargaining over wages and benefits. The bill would give employers a role in approving the process by which their own employees vote to strike.
A failed recertification election would terminate an existing collective bargaining contract, which could disrupt labor relations even for employers that signed the contract in good faith.
